global_app_rules: Prefer a smaller finished app over a larger half-built app.
Every generated app must have real user-visible behavior, not only placeholder screens.
For iOS apps, default to SwiftUI, deterministic local state first, Apple system frameworks, and no third-party package unless it materially reduces risk.
Every screen needs empty, loading, success, and error states when the workflow can reach those states.
Treat accessibility, privacy, persistence, and testing as product requirements, not polish.
Do not declare the app done until build verification and the final review agree on what works and what remains limited.

rules: Preserve the user's original prompt before interpreting it.
Convert the prompt into hard requirements, non-goals, output shape, quality bar, and decision rules.
Resolve conflicts by naming the assumption, not by silently changing the assignment.
required_output: Original prompt excerpt or full prompt reference.
acceptance_checks: A later phase can tell whether it is violating the user's prompt.
Multi-app quantity/category requirements are explicit.
Production-ready means more than a prototype or spec.

rules: Infer the likely audience, competing alternatives, platform expectations, and risky unknowns from the prompt.
If facts are uncertain, label them as assumptions rather than pretending external research was performed.
Decide what would make the app feel native and valuable on iPhone, not just technically possible.
required_output: Comparable apps or patterns to learn from.
acceptance_checks: The next phase can use the output without repeating discovery.
At least three concrete risks or unknowns are named.
The research points toward a shippable first version.

rules: If the prompt asks for multiple apps, each selected app must be an independent sibling project.
Do not let one idea dominate the portfolio; give category-specific opinions before converging.
Emit portfolio-json when the prompt is a portfolio parent, and set build=true for every selected app when the prompt asks for production-ready apps.
required_output: Selected app list with category, slug, promise, target user, and build flag.
acceptance_checks: The selected app count matches the prompt or explains any explicit reduction.
Each selected app can become a separate folder.
No requested category is silently collapsed into another app.

rules: Turn the user's prompt into one precise product promise.
Name the primary user, the job-to-be-done, the core loop, and the non-goals.
Resolve ambiguity decisively when the prompt is underspecified.
acceptance_checks: A developer could explain the app in one sentence.
The scope is small enough to build in one pass.
Out-of-scope items are explicit.

rules: Write a concrete brief for this specific app, not a generic category description.
Explain why users would pay and what the subscription unlocks as real utility.
Include local-first behavior and a future cloud path without making cloud a dependency for v1.
acceptance_checks: The app's value is specific enough to build.
Subscription value is functional, not cosmetic.
The brief can drive design without more ideation.

rules: Find the smallest end-to-end slice that proves the concept.
Keep the slice emotionally satisfying, not just technically minimal.
Prefer one polished workflow over many shallow features.
acceptance_checks: The MVP can be built by the later build phase without new product debate.
The slice includes at least one complete user workflow.

rules: Enumerate edge cases before features expand.
Identify privacy, data-loss, offline, notification, and permission concerns where relevant.
Convert open questions into assumptions or explicit exclusions.
acceptance_checks: No major ambiguity remains for design or architecture.
Risks have concrete mitigations or are named as limitations.

rules: Prioritize ruthlessly with must/should/could/won't.
Every must-have feature needs a user story and acceptance criteria.
Do not include features that cannot fit the chosen build size.
acceptance_checks: All must-have features support the product promise.
The build phase can complete the must-have list.

rules: Design real screens and states, not vague UX language.
Make navigation, empty states, errors, onboarding, and persistence visible.
Use iOS-native patterns unless the prompt clearly demands otherwise.
acceptance_checks: A SwiftUI developer can create the view hierarchy from this output.
Every required user workflow has a screen/state path.

rules: Produce a builder-ready design handoff, not visual adjectives.
If external Claude Design is desired, provide a clean prompt/upload plan the user can use directly.
Every primary screen must include layout intent, key components, state variants, accessibility, and motion guidance.
required_output: Claude Design prompt or explicit no-external-design decision.
acceptance_checks: A SwiftUI builder can implement the interface from the handoff.
The handoff does not depend on hidden design decisions.
The design direction is premium and category-specific.

rules: Review the product through iOS-specific constraints before tech_specs locks implementation.
Prefer SwiftUI, Apple frameworks, local persistence, and permissive dependencies only.
Call out privacy, permissions, offline behavior, StoreKit, ML/AR feasibility, and testability.
acceptance_checks: The app can be built as a native iOS app without vague architecture gaps.
Any ML, LLM, or AR use is justified by user value.
No dependency violates the permissive-license policy.

rules: Choose the simplest architecture that supports the MVP and tests.
Specify data models, services, persistence, concurrency boundaries, and error handling.
Prefer Apple frameworks and permissive dependencies only.
Emit the required interfaces-json block.
acceptance_checks: Parallel build lanes can work without inventing incompatible types.
The spec names how the app will be built and verified.

rules: Sequence work by dependency, not by role preference.
Keep the plan aligned to the actual build lanes.
Include verification and repair time as first-class work.
acceptance_checks: The plan is executable by the task assignment phase.
Testing and integration are not left to the end as vague polish.

rules: Create build tasks that map cleanly to the fixed lane ids.
Each task must own files, dependencies, and acceptance criteria.
Avoid overlapping file ownership except for integrator-owned files.
Emit the required tasks-json block.
acceptance_checks: No task is ownerless.
Dependencies are acyclic.
The build workers can start immediately.

rules: Act as the final pre-build gate, not another planning brainstorm.
Check consistency across prompt contract, product brief, design handoff, iOS architecture, tech specs, project plan, and tasks.
Resolve contradictions by downgrading scope or naming a blocker before code starts.
acceptance_checks: The build phase can start without inventing product/design/architecture decisions.
Every major workflow has an acceptance criterion.
Testing responsibilities are explicit.

rules: Build real files in app_build; do not only describe the solution.
Keep changes scoped to the assigned lane and leave integration files to the integrator.
Every iteration should reduce compile, runtime, or product-completeness risk.
When generating iOS, include unit/UI test targets where feasible.
acceptance_checks: The app has a runnable entry point.
The main user workflow is implemented.
The integrator has wired lane outputs together.

rules: Run or interpret the real verifier results; do not claim success without tool evidence.
Repair compile/test failures with minimal changes in app_build.
Record honest remaining blockers when the verifier cannot pass.
required_output: Next repair step if still failing.
acceptance_checks: The phase contains real verification evidence or a clear reason it could not run.
Failures are tied to concrete files/errors.
No new feature work is introduced during repair.

rules: Cover every important workflow, not only the happy path.
Include simulator/device steps, expected results, and regression checks.
Include accessibility, persistence, permissions, offline behavior, and subscription/paywall checks when relevant.
acceptance_checks: A human can run the checklist without asking what to tap.
Every core feature from app_features appears in QA.
Failure states are tested, not ignored.

rules: Prepare launch material and review risk assessment, not marketing fluff.
Treat privacy labels, permission strings, subscriptions, support, and review blockers as required launch work.
Do not mark launch-ready when verification or QA still has blockers.
acceptance_checks: The app has an honest launch-readiness verdict.
Privacy and permissions are specific.
Subscription value and compliance risks are explicit.

rules: Judge the app against the original prompt, the MVP slice, and verification results.
Do not hide unfinished work.
Separate launch blockers from nice-to-have follow-up.
acceptance_checks: The review is honest enough for a user to decide whether to run or iterate.
Every blocker has an owner or a concrete next step.

rules: For portfolio parents, validate the actual folder/project shape against the user's requested app count/categories.
For portfolio children, validate parent metadata and workflow selection.
For single-app runs, explicitly mark the audit not applicable instead of inventing portfolio work.
acceptance_checks: A multi-app parent cannot pass if selected apps were collapsed into one project folder.
Every child has an initial prompt and workflow.
Any mismatch is recorded as a blocker.
